claimReview.hardDependencies: All four direct claims have no hard prerequisites in this frozen graph; no edge or automatic mastery transfer is introduced. General inquiry/map methods remain separate from these factual claims.
claimReview.researchBoundary: Original guides and factual source checks are retained unchanged, including their low teaching-confidence and source-perspective limits; this reuse review is not a classroom study.

preparation: Adult setup: supply the actual original attributed case packets at the resource pointers, with author/institution, actual source URL, date, place and known/unknown fields. Read usable passages rather than make pupils guess facts. The existing packets include actual facts, not merely instructions to invent cases.

Use an attributed current locator and dated time strip to distinguish historical locations from present boundaries, and a comparison organizer with economic/political/cultural/social evidence headings. These are factual-knowledge task supports; this batch does not add a new map/inquiry association.

Retain the complete whole-claim study and independent checks above. For this Grade 6 source task, use the selected cases in the protocols below; do not infer all unrelated community histories, every learner’s identity, current rights or an individual’s experience from success.

actions: Using the dated New France cases, describe actual political appointment/administration, land/work obligations, Catholic religion and school/care relationships. Connect the French crown/colonial official arrangement and Catholic institutional practices explicitly with the French settler-origin context, rather than infer origin from a modern surname.

Add the Traill household’s attributed 1832–35 work/food/family account and Buxton’s 1849–50 land, security and schooling account as distinct later settler settings. Use the actual source-supported ordinary-life details; do not treat a prescriptive outsider description as every person’s daily schedule.

For the applicable Indigenous relationship, use the actual Great Lakes trade and Port-Royal packets: settler commercial/settlement/religious aims depended on Indigenous expertise and relationships, while trade/alliance, epidemics and conflict affected named communities. Describe a particular supported impact; a colonial grant/map does not establish empty land or extinguished rights.
successEvidence: Actual economic, political, cultural and social aspects are described with distinct dates/places; a supported origin-culture influence is explained and an applicable Indigenous impact is not omitted.
nearMisses: Lists only farm objects or religion without the political/social relationship, or claims all residents shared belief/access.
Turns settler ambition into Indigenous consent or repeats prejudicial source judgments.
settler-life-and-origin.transfer: Use a new original fictional late-seventeenth-century Québec account: a household needs milling access and a parish marriage record while officials dispute fortification spending. Identify relevant learned relationships and the French-colonial context, then state what the account cannot establish about an Indigenous community or universal access.

actions: Actually analyse more than one distinct community: the Great Lakes Wendat trade/alliance/epidemic relationship and later Mattawa/Nipissing Métis collective emergence are required selected comparisons; retain the Qikiqtani 1576–78 encounter as a third distinct perspective, not a representative of all Inuit.

For each, identify a particular development, place and approximate period, then explain a supported effect on community relationships, life or collective development/identity. Distinguish earlier trade/kinship conditions from late-1700s/early-1800s Métis collective emergence, not an ancestry test.

Compare benefits and harms without cancelling coercion because useful objects were exchanged; state the difference between the English suspicion about missing sailors and the attributed Inuit oral history.
successEvidence: At least two actual named communities and event/development → development/identity relationships, with source limits and chronology; all three selected cases are used in this programme.
nearMisses: Names two explorers without explaining community effects.
Calls all mixed-ancestry families Métis or presents the missing-sailor suspicion as proven.
indigenous-developments.transfer: Offer the existing original early-family versus later Mattawa-network comparison; explain which collective-history conclusion is supported and why a name, mixed ancestry or a tool exchange cannot establish current identity/rights.

actions: Actually compare Black Buxton/Elgin’s 1849 founding and 1849–50 home/farm/school development with Jewish Lower Canada political exclusion/change and Toronto’s 1922–23 hospital founding. These are more than one settler/newcomer community, not simply two places in one history.

Explain how each selected event/development affected community opportunities, security, collective action or relationships. Use the actual mission/Parks accounts and Hart/Toronto cases, including hospital care beyond its founders’ community.
Keep Buxton’s later 1859 school separate from 1850 literacy teaching, and do not say racism ended, all Jewish people were immigrants, or community achievements had to earn rights.
successEvidence: At least the actual Black and Jewish community histories, each with significant development and explained effect on community development/identity, are assessed.
nearMisses: Only lists founding years, or attributes later school buildings to 1849.
Says the existence of a hospital ended discrimination or made its founders deserving of rights.
settler-developments.transfer: A fictional museum caption says that Buxton education and Toronto hospital care prove all Canadian communities then had equal access. Use the actual dated cases to correct the inference and state what each does establish.

actions: Describe actual relationships among newcomers and earlier residents using the Great Lakes/Wendat–French trade and Mi’kmaq–French Port-Royal cases; explain the parties, exchanged knowledge/materials, dependence, cooperation and supported harms.

Contrast the 1701 multilateral peace/diplomatic relationship with the later Toronto hospital example of responding to professional/care exclusion and serving beyond the founding community. The latter is not backdated or presented as an Indigenous treaty.
Keep relationships between communities distinct from assumptions about every individual; current colonial/title or legal adequacy verdicts are not derived from these historical accounts.
successEvidence: Describes several actual intercommunity interactions and supported consequences, including newcomers and existing communities; agency and chronology remain distinct.
nearMisses: Describes isolated communities without any relationship, or says all exchanges were equal/harmless.
between-community-interactions.transfer: Use the retained original new-trader/route scenario: explain why existing relationships and local expertise matter and why receiving metal tools does not establish consent, cultural disappearance or surrender.

actions: Compare a few actual communities using a source-bound table: Anishinaabe Kaministiquia early-1800s mobility/food/trade, the Traill household’s 1832–35 clearing/farm/provisioning work, Black Buxton 1849–50 security/education development, and the New France religious/landholding or Jewish Toronto care case.

Identify supported economic, social and cultural differences rather than rank cultures. Attach each fact to its date/place/source; non-contemporaneous cases can show differences but cannot alone establish one universal causal evolution.

Include the bounded source-documented men/women/children contributions from the complete period repertoire where used; do not extrapolate a particular role or observer account to every member, to all First Nations or to children today.
successEvidence: A few actual communities, including the named First Nation case, have concrete social/cultural/economic differences explained from evidence rather than a generic past/present label.
nearMisses: Makes a superiority ranking, generalises one household to a whole people, or treats missing documentation as absence.
community-differences.transfer: After learning, offer one fresh attributed detail from the supplied packet with its date/place: explain which comparison it changes, what remains unknown and why it cannot simply be assigned to every historical community.

coverageBoundary: Source-fit authoring designs for the five listed expectations, not completed learner work or whole-Grade-6 completion. A1/A2/A3 overall and the other unresolved A duties are not promoted by these five tasks.
